senses.def: a container, primarily for liquids or wet objects
senses.comment: The vessels referred to in this context would have been relatively small, containing probably not more than a liter (about a quart).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to not being right or just
the content of legal charges brought against someone
pertaining to being in accordance with historical fact
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘the truth’ may be rendered simply as ‘what really is’ or ‘what is so’ or ‘what has happened.’

senses.def: pertaining to being real and not imaginary
senses.comment: The figurative or symbolic sense of this statement does not, of course, take away from its reality.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being truthful and honest
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must translate ἀληθής in Matthew 22:16 as ‘you always say what is true.’

senses.def: creeping plant that develops a woody stem when it matures; Vitis vinifera; grows along the ground until it finds a tree or other object to climb, using tendrils; bears bunches of small round fruit that are sweet and juicy; symbol of blessing, prosperity, and happiness
senses.comment: A rendering of ἄμπελος as ‘vine’ rather than as ‘grapevine’ in John 15:1 may cause serious misunderstanding, since it might refer merely to a vine which does not produce fruit. Accordingly, if there is no particular expression for ‘grapevine,’ it may be more satisfactory in John 15:1 to speak of ‘fruit bush’ or ‘fruit plant.’ A term in John 15:1 which would indicate only jungle vines would also result in complete misunderstanding of the function of pruning (see 43.12), since such jungle vines are never pruned and in fact are only useful when they have been cut down and used for building purposes.|In some languages a grapevine may be referred to as ‘a bush producing grapes,’ and in certain other languages it is called ‘the wine plant.’

senses.def: to shout or cry out, with the possible implication of the unpleasant nature of the sound
pertaining to what cannot be uttered or expressed
glosses: what cannot be expressed in words

senses.def: to resist by actively opposing pressure or power
senses.comment: In a number of languages one may appropriately translate ‘to resist’ in a number of contexts as ‘to fight back against’ or ‘to oppose in return.’ In some contexts, however, such as Acts 7:51, the meaning may perhaps be best expressed by a negation, for example, ‘you have never been willing to yield to the Holy Spirit.’

senses.def: unwillingness or refusal to comply with the demands of some authority
to refuse to believe the Christian message
glosses: to refuse to be a believer
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἀπείθεια in Ephesians 2:2 as overt disobedience to God (see 36.23).

senses.def: an official decision, frequently involving a legal verdict
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 1:9 ἀπόκριμα is used figuratively; no actual official decision had been made, but in view of all of the difficulties which Paul and his colleagues had suffered, it seemed as though such an official decision had been rendered.

senses.def: pertaining to not being capable of being approached
senses.comment: It may be necessary to indicate, either in the text or in a marginal note, the reason why the light cannot be approached, for one could interpret this passage to mean that the light was either so small as not to be generally visible or so far away that it could not be reached. If, however, one uses a term for ‘light’ which implies extreme intensity of light, then the context should indicate the basis for its being unapproachable.

senses.def: pertaining to having been born recently
senses.comment: ‘Newly born babies’ may be rendered as ‘babies who have just been born’ or ‘babies who have just begun to live.’

senses.def: pertaining to a lack of capacity for insight and understanding
senses.comment: Care must be exercised in the rendering of ἀσύνετος in Matthew 15:16 and Romans 1:21, since a lack of capacity for understanding may result from mental deficiencies or from a lack of the proper use of mental capacity. It is, of course, this latter meaning which is involved in the use of ἀσύνετος in these contexts.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀφικνέομαι ‘to move up to a point,’ not occurring in the NT) to become known as the result of information reaching its destination
to punish by physical torture or torment
(derivative of βιόω ‘to live,’ 41.18) pertaining to daily life or existence
(derivative of Γάδαρα ‘Gadara,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Gadara
a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see 14.36)
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of Luke 23:44 ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

senses.def: a state of fear because of a lack of courage or moral strength
senses.comment: ‘Cowardice’ is often rendered by means of an idiom, for example, ‘to have a fallen heart,’ ‘to have a soft heart,’ or ‘one’s heart has disappeared.’

senses.def: to obtain accurate and thorough information about
to make a judgment on legal matters, with the implication of thorough examination
glosses: to arrive at a verdict after examination

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: to rescue completely from danger
to cause someone to become well again after having been sick
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

senses.def: a corrected new order, implying a change from an earlier state
senses.comment: μέχρι καιροῦ διορθώσεως can be translated as ‘until the time of the new order’ Hebrews 9:10, but see 62.6 for the generally preferred interpretation.

senses.def: the process of establishing a new order
senses.comment: μέχρι καιροῦ διορθώσεως ‘until the time when he will establish a new order’ or ‘… will reform all things’ Hebrews 9:10, but see 62.5.

senses.def: pertaining to that which is difficult to bear or endure
that which provides the basis or foundation for belief or practice
to provide detailed information in a systematic manner

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: a state of eagerness involving perseverance over a period of time
to look forward with confidence to that which is good and beneficial
to expect, with the implication of some benefit
to enter secretly and with ulterior motives
senses.comment: In order to render the meaning of ἐνδύνω in 2 Timothy 3:6, it may be necessary in some languages to be somewhat more explicit, for example, ‘they enter into houses without being seen’ or ‘they enter into houses without people knowing what they really intend to do.’

senses.def: to take something out of its place

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: to rescue or set someone free from danger

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to choose out from among
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret ἐξαιρέομαι in Acts 26:17 as meaning ‘to rescue from’ (see 21.17).

senses.def: to experience or feel shame or disgrace because of some particular event or activity
to try to learn the location of something by searching for it (presumably somewhat more emphatic or goal-directed than in the case of ζητέω[a] ‘to try to learn where something is,’ 27.41)
glosses: to try to find out by looking for

senses.def: to desire to have or experience something, with the probable implication of making an attempt to realize one’s desire
to return to a point or area where one has been before, with probable emphasis on turning about
to change one’s belief, with focus upon that to which one turns
senses.comment: In analyzing the meaning of στρέφω[g], ἐπιστρέφω[b], and ἐπιστροφή[a] in such passages as Galatians 4:9 and 1 Peter 2:25, it is difficult to determine the extent to which belief or behavior is primarily in focus. In the case of 1 Peter 2:25, one could certainly argue that the emphasis is upon the interpersonal relationship. It is therefore essential in rendering these terms not to narrow the meaning too much, for in this way one would certainly do violence to certain crucial semantic features.

senses.def: to cause a person to change belief, with focus upon that to which one turns
to change one’s manner of life in a particular direction, with the implication of turning back to God
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not sufficient to simply translate ‘to change one’s manner of life,’ for this could either be neutral or even suggest a change for the worse. Therefore, it may be necessary in a number of instances to translate ‘to change one’s way of living as God would want’ or ‘to change and live like God would want one to live.’

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to turn hearts to) to cause a change of attitude in a positive and acceptable direction
to turn around to or toward
general word for reptile that includes snakes and lizards
senses.comment: Though ἑρπετόν is often interpreted as referring only to snakes, it also includes in biblical contexts (as the result of the influence of classifications based on Hebrew terminology, as in a number of small four-footed animals as well as snakes, for example, rats, mice, frogs, toads, salamanders, and lizards. However, in the various NT contexts (for example Acts 10:12 where ‘creeping things’ are contrasted with birds, animals, and fish) it is probably more satisfactory to use a term which designates primarily snakes. In a number of languages a very important distinction is made between four-footed reptiles (such as lizards) and snakes. If such a distinction is made, it is then probably better to use a term which designates only snakes, since a term for ‘animals’ will probably also include lizards.

senses.def: pertaining to being generous in sharing

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: the continuous extent of time up to a point
senses.comment: The phrase εἰ μὴ ὅταν is often translated as ‘until’ (for example, μηδενὶ ἅ εἶδον διηγήσωνταιεἰ μὴ ὅταν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ ‘not to tell anybody what they have seen until the Son of Man has risen from death’ Mark 9:9), but this phrase may be analyzed as meaning ‘if it is not when,’ an expression which is semantically equivalent to ‘until.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time
extension up to or as far as a goal

senses.subdomain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
senses.def: a degree extending to a particular point as marked by the context
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to express in a succinct manner a degree which reaches to a particular point. The same meaning, however, may often be expressed in a somewhat different form. For example, in Matthew 26:38 one may translate ‘my soul is very sorrowful; it is just as though I were dying.’

senses.def: the extent of a quantity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to restructure somewhat the expression ‘up to half of my kingdom,’ for example, ‘I will give you half of my kingdom but not more than half.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout
senses.def: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: the political followers and adherents to Herod the Great and his family
a state of a relatively high degree of heat
the father of Enoch in the genealogy of Jesus
a soldier who fights on horseback
to be fitting or right, with the implication of possible moral judgment involved
the visible gases and particles given off by burning matter; varies in appearance from white to black and rises in the air

to reestablish proper friendly interpersonal relations after these have been disrupted or broken (the componential features of this series of meanings involve (1) disruption of friendly relations because of (2) presumed or real provocation (3) overt behavior designed to remove hostility, and (4) restoration of original friendly relations)
glosses: to make things right with one another
senses.comment: Because of the variety and complexity of the components involved in reconciliation, it is often necessary to use an entire phrase in order to communicate satisfactorily the meanings of the terms in this subdomain. In some languages, however, reconciliation is often spoken of in idiomatic terms, for example, ‘to cause to become friends again,’ ‘to cause to snap fingers again’ (a symbol of friendly interpersonal relations in many parts of Africa), ‘to cause to be one again,’ or ‘to take away the separation.’ A particularly crucial element in terms for reconciliation is the assigning of responsibility for original guilt in causing the estrangement. Some terms, for example, imply that the individual who initiates reconciliation is by doing so admitting his guilt in causing the estrangement. This, of course, provides a completely untenable meaning for reconciliation in speaking of God reconciling people to himself through Christ.|In a number of languages the contextual basis for an expression for reconciliation is often found in terms relating to the reconciliation of husbands and wives. Such expressions fit in well with many contexts in the Scriptures, especially in speaking of reconciliation of people to God, since God is frequently referred to as the husband and the believers as the wife.

senses.def: to make use of instruments
to conduct oneself in such a way as to become completely occupied by certain means
to gain by means of one’s activity or investment
to cause a loss not to happen
to be tossed back and forth by the motion of waves
glosses: to be tossed about by waves
senses.comment: The imagery in Ephesians 4:14 is based upon a person in a boat being tossed about by the waves. It may, therefore, be necessary to introduce a boat or ship in the context.

senses.def: a relatively large basket used primarily for food or produce
senses.comment: Translators often find it difficult to obtain satisfactory equivalents of σπυρίς (6.149) and κόφινος, since in various receptor languages there are highly specific terms for particular kinds of baskets depending upon type of construction and size. Unfortunately, there is no way of determining from the Greek text precisely the size or type of baskets involved in references to σπυρίς and κόφινος.

senses.def: a city on the coast of north Africa
an alternative form of Λευί[a], 93.231 (Luke 5:29)
to release or set free, with the implied analogy to the process of freeing a slave
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot speak of ‘being set free’ without specifying the particular manner or circumstances involved. In the case of Luke 24:21, for example, it may be necessary to translate ‘to liberate Israel’ as ‘to cause Israel to be free from foreign control’ or ‘… from the power of Rome.’ A similar type of translation may be required in Luke 2:38, but in the case of Ephesians 1:7 it may be necessary to specify ‘we are set free from sin’ or ‘we are set free from our bad desires.’

senses.def: to provide information about a person or an event concerning which the speaker has direct knowledge
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is necessary to indicate specifically what is the content of a witness, so that, for example, in Luke 21:13 it may be necessary to say ‘this is your chance to witness to the good news’ or ‘… to tell about the good news’ or ‘… to tell what you yourselves know about the good news.’

senses.def: (derivative of μαρτυρέω[a] ‘to witness,’ 33.262) the content of what is witnessed or said
senses.comment: In a number of languages one must specify the content of the witness, and it also may be necessary to indicate the agent who is engaged in the witnessing. For example, in Mark 14:55 it may be necessary to translate ‘they tried to find someone who would testify against Jesus’ or ‘… say something against Jesus.’ In 1 Corinthians 1:6 it may be necessary to translate ‘what we told you from personal experience about Christ has become so firmly fixed in you’ or ‘… has become so much a part of you.’

senses.def: (derivative of μαρτυρέω[b] to speak well of, 33.263) that which is said about a person on the basis of an evaluation of the persons conduct
senses.comment: In obtaining a satisfactory equivalent for ‘reputation,’ it may be necessary to restructure considerably the clause in which a term such as μαρτυρία[c] or ὄνομα[c] occurs. For example, in 1 Timothy 3:7 one may translate ‘he should be the kind of man that people outside the church say is a good person.’ Similarly, in Revelation 3:1 one may need to translate ‘people speak of you as being alive even though you are dead.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Units of Time: Daybreak, Midday, Midnight, Late
senses.def: the midpoint of a day
senses.comment: In a number of languages μεσημβρία[a] may be rendered as ‘when the sun is high’ or ‘when the sun is above one’s head’ or ‘just as the sun starts down.’ For another interpretation of μεσημβρία in Acts 8:26, see 82.4.
It is also possible to interpret κατὰ μεσημβρίαν in Acts 8:26 as meaning ‘about noon,’ since μεσημβρία is a normal expression for ‘midday’ or ‘noon’ (see 67.74). See also the discussion at 82.3.

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the part of the leg above the knee
to produce a loud, roaring, or bellowing noise, typically of oxen, but also applicable to other large animals

senses.subdomain: Land in Contrast With the Sea

senses.def: to cause something to become dry
(derivative of ξηρός[a] ‘dry,’ 79.80) to become dry
senses.comment: It may be more appropriate in a number of languages to translate this clause in Mark 5:29 as ‘and immediately her menstrual bleeding stopped.’

senses.def: (derivative of ξηρός[a] ‘dry,’ 79.80) to become ripe, with reference to grain which dries in the process of ripening
(a figurative extension of meaning of ξηραίνομαι[a] ‘to dry up,’ 79.81) to become stiff to the point of not being able to move
senses.comment: In some languages one may express the meaning of ‘to be stiff all over’ as ‘not able to move any part of the body.’

senses.def: (derivative of ὀλοθρεύω ‘to destroy, to ruin,’ 20.34) one who causes destruction
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 10:10 ὀλοθρευτής may serve as a title referring to a destroying angel or even to Satan.

senses.def: pertaining to that which can be seen
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be wise to render ‘visible and invisible’ as an active expression with ‘people’ as the subject, for example, ‘all things were created by him … both those things which people can see and those things which people cannot see’ or ‘… what people can see and what they cannot see.’

senses.def: a person greeted in Romans 16:9
extension from a source, involving all possible points
all possible positions
to watch closely or diligently
to keep or maintain a tradition or custom
a person greeted in Romans 16:14
protective armor covering the head; used in battle
senses.comment: For languages having no term for helmet, one may use a descriptive equivalent such as ‘a protection for the head’ or ‘a covering for the head in fighting.’ The phrase τὴν περικεφαλαίαν τοῦ σωτηρίου δέξασθε may then be translated as ‘accept salvation as something like a protection for the head.’

senses.def: to be sick with a fever
senses.comment: Though in a number of languages one can say ‘a person has a fever,’ in some languages the reverse expression is used, for example, ‘the fever has a person.’ Similarly, instead of saying ‘a person has a disease,’ it is ‘the disease which grabs a person.’ One may often speak of a fever as ‘to become hot’ or ‘to burn’ or ‘to be sick with burning.’|It is also possible to understand πίμπρημι in Acts 28:6 as a process of swelling up (see 23.163).
It is also possible to understand πίμπρημι in Acts 28:6 as being sick with a fever (see 23.159).

senses.def: extension from a source, with an incorporated interrogative point of reference
a marker of an event indicating how something took place
interrogative expressions of reason

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: drinking parties involving unrestrained indulgence in alcoholic beverages and accompanying immoral behavior

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause provocation or irritation in someone
to strike against something, with the implication of resistance or damage
senses.comment: The focus in Matthew 4:6 is upon the result of striking a foot against a stone, and therefore one may translate ‘to hurt your foot by striking it against a stone.’

senses.def: to strike one’s foot against something as one walks and in this way to lose one’s balance temporarily
to take offense, with the implication of a feeling of repugnance or rejection
senses.comment: This expression in Romans 14:21 may, however, be restructured and translated as ‘which will cause your brother to become offended’ or ‘which will cause your brother to feel repugnance (because of what you have done).’ In some instances the closest equivalent of προσκόπτω may be ‘to feel bad against.’

senses.def: first in a temporal sequence
a woman of Jericho mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus; see 93.306
an island in the northern Aegean Sea
generally regarded as the same person as Σιλᾶς (93.339)
a city located near the Dead Sea and destroyed because of its evil; possible identification with Tel Hammam, northeast of the Dead Sea
(derivative of στέφανος[b] ‘prize, reward,’ 57.121) to cause someone to receive a prize or reward as the result of excellence in competition

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of στεφανόω ‘to crown’ or ‘to put a victory wreath on,’ not occurring in the NT with this meaning) to show particular honor to a person as the result of some type of victory
to associate with one another, normally involving spacial proximity and/or joint activity, and usually implying some kind of reciprocal relation or involvement
glosses: to be in the company of
senses.comment: In translating terms referring to association, one may employ a number of different kinds of expressions, for example, ‘to have something to do with,’ ‘to keep company with,’ ‘to go around with,’ ‘to join in doing things together,’ or ‘to become a companion of.’ Sometimes association is spoken of in terms of the impression made upon others, for example, ‘to be seen often together,’ ‘to be regarded as close friends,’ and even idiomatically as ‘to be another person’s shadow.’|Some scholars interpret συγχράομαι in John 4:9 as denoting the use of the same dishes or utensils, so that one may translate this expression in John 4:9 as ‘Jews do not use dishes together with Samaritans’ or ‘Jews and Samaritans do not use the same dishes.’ Such an interpretation, however, is based upon etymological arguments for which there seems to be no certain justification in general Greek usage.

senses.def: pertaining to similarity of attitude and spirit
to converse with someone, including a clear implication as to reciprocal response

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: (derivative of σῴζω[a] ‘to rescue, to save,’ 21.18) one who rescues or saves
(derivative of σῴζω[b] ‘to save,’ 21.27) one who saves
an unusual sign, especially one in the heavens, serving to foretell impending events
senses.comment: In ancient times a portent might consist of a particular arrangement of the planets, an unusual display of northern lights, a conspicuous comet, or a cluster of falling stars. For a discussion of σημεῖον ‘sign,’ see 33.477.

senses.def: the condition resulting from being severely hurt or wounded

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to maltreat in an insolent manner
senses.comment: In a number of contexts ὑβρίζω seems to combine not only the maltreatment of persons but the attitude of insolence on the part of the one who maltreats another. Therefore, it may be useful in some instances to employ a double expression, for example, ‘to look down upon and to maltreat.’

senses.def: to speak against someone in an insolent and arrogant way

senses.subdomain: Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
senses.def: a model of behavior as an example to be imitated or to be avoided
the father of Anna the prophetess
pertaining to having affection for one’s own offspring
to communicate directly or indirectly to someone who is presumably at a distance, in order to tell such a person to come
to speak with considerable volume or loudness
to use an attribution in speaking of a person
senses.comment: It is not always possible to determine from the context whether the act involved is an initial naming of a person or simply calling a person by a particular name. Likewise in the case of attributions or titles, it is not always possible to determine whether it is a matter of giving an attribution or title to a person or simply a matter of speaking of or to a person by means of such an attribution or title. In some instances the giving of a title may be made indirect. For example, in Matthew 1:23 the statement ‘and they will call his name Emmanuel’ suggests the giving of a title, but the process is stated in terms of how people will speak of this person.

senses.def: to ask a person to accept offered hospitality
to produce a sound
senses.comment: Though in Matthew 26:75 one may wish to use a more specific term such as ‘crows,’ the meaning of φωνέω[e] is simply ‘to produce a sound.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the bitter yellowish liquid secreted by the liver and stored in the gall bladder
senses.comment: It is possible, however, that in Matthew 27:34 the reference is not specifically to gall but to a substance with an especially unpleasant taste.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be in the gall of bitterness) to be particularly envious or resentful of someone
a small stone, possibly used for casting a vote or as a magical amulet
senses.comment: A number of different suggestions have been made as to the reference of ψῆφος in Revelation 2:17. Some scholars believe that the white ψῆφος indicates a vote of acquittal in court. Others contend that it is simply a magical amulet; still others, a token of Roman hospitality; and finally, some have suggested that it may represent a ticket to the gladiatorial games, that is to say, to martyrdom. The context, however, suggests clearly that this is something to be prized and a type of reward for those who have ‘won the victory.’
